newsitem.title: UK: Oil firms look to bacteria for refinery advances.
newsitem.headline: Oil firms look to bacteria for refinery advances.

text.p: Oil companies are developing biological catalysts in what may prove to be the biggest breakthrough in oil refining for 25 years, an oil expert said on Thursday.
Bacteria rather than inert chemicals are being developed to act as catalysts in the oil refining process to help boost profits and produce cleaner oil products.
Catalysts are materials used by refineries to accelerate reactions in the conversion process that turns crude oil into high value oil products such as petrol.
But oil companies are under environmental pressure to reduce the sulphur content of their products because the chemical is a major pollutant.

"There have been few genuinely new (catalytic) materials discovered over the past few decades and if bio-desulphurisation works it will be a major step," said Dr Graham Butler, senior technology advisor at British Petroleum Oil International .

"The importance of radical technologies such as biocatalysis and gas conversion will be very difficult to judge in terms of viability and penetration, but could start to break through into the mainstream of refining," Butler told conference delegates at the Institute of Petroleum in London.

Butler said hydroskimming refineries -- plants that hardly use catalysts at all -- are no longer viable and that all major western refineries now relied on the catalytic process to be both competitive and to meet environmental regulations.
The last significant new step in catalysts was the development of ZSM 5 zeolite in the early 1970s with all subsequent improvements more akin to fine tuning than breaking fresh ground, said Butler.

But the potential emergence of biocatalysts could change that. A company called Environmental Biosystems (EBS) is working with two oil majors into developing a biodesulphurisation process that will use bacteria as a catalyst to take sulphur out of crude and middle distillates.
Research into the wellhead biodesulphurisation of crude could have a large impact on refinery investments and configurations if a viable process becomes available, said Butler.

"Most pundits on crude supply suggest that in time heavier, sourer crudes will be increasingly prevalent and that more cost effective catalytic processes to deal with residue upgrading are still required."
The widespread use of biocatalysts is still some way in the future as technological and cost constraints have yet to be overcome.

"Biocatalytic processes take a lot longer than conventional catalysts, but if they could be speeded by genetic engineering then they have real potential as catalysts within a refining framework," Butler told Reuters.
Progress has been made in converting gas to extremely clean refined oil products.

In the 1980s the technology was introduced on a relatively small commercial scale by Shell in Malaysia and Mossgas in South Africa, but there are now signs the technology is becoming more attractive with Exxon Corp , Shell and Sasol Ltd all looking at 30-50,000 barrels per day plants.
